sources.section: §1.1 Two cross-cutting distinctions: scalar vs non-scalar, equality vs inequality

rules.statement: Scalar comparison evaluates relative positions on a gradable scale, whereas non-scalar comparison concerns identity, difference, likeness, or unlikeness rather than degree.
rules.condition: Classify a comparison as scalar when the compared property permits degrees on a scale; classify it as non-scalar when the relation is primarily sameness or difference of entities or kinds instead of graded magnitude.

contrast.text: Asha is as tall as Noam. [scalar comparison of height]
Asha is taller than Noam. [scalar difference of degree]
We took the same shuttle as yesterday. [non-scalar comparison of identity]
We took a different shuttle from yesterday. [non-scalar comparison of non-identity]

sources.section: §1.1 Two cross-cutting distinctions: scalar vs non-scalar, equality vs inequality

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Burton-Roberts source material and concept index were not available for comparison; no Burton-Roberts position is inferred.

rules.review_notes: The scalar/non-scalar distinction concerns comparison of degree versus identity/likeness. Scalar comparative inflection is central, but the source does not treat all comparative forms as an inflectional suffix. Owner approved; independent second-pass review outstanding.

rules.concept: equality versus inequality in scalar and non-scalar comparison
rules.statement: Equality and inequality cross-cut scalar and non-scalar comparisons: scalar relations concern degrees, while non-scalar relations concern sameness or likeness versus difference; as marks major equality patterns and than certain inequality patterns.
rules.condition: When assigning equality or inequality, first determine whether the relation is scalar or non-scalar: an as ... as degree comparison and same ... as identity comparison both fall in the equality category, whereas -er/more ... than and different ... from/other ... than illustrate inequality.

exceptions.description: The preposition than with different is available in some varieties of English; do not generalise its distribution or reject its use outright.

contrast.text: Mara is as strong as Jo. [scalar equality]
Mara is stronger than Jo. [scalar inequality]
This is the same model as the earlier prototype. [non-scalar equality]
This is a different model from the earlier prototype. [non-scalar inequality]
The design is different than the earlier prototype. [non-scalar inequality; accepted in some varieties]

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: equality versus inequality in scalar and non-scalar comparison
burton_roberts_mapping.note: Burton-Roberts source material and concept index were not available for comparison; no Burton-Roberts position is inferred.

rules.review_notes: The source treats equality/inequality as grammatical labels across the two dimensions. Non-scalar same does not imply numerical equality. Different than is explicitly variety-sensitive; owner-approved, no independent second pass.

rules.concept: superiority versus inferiority in scalar inequality
rules.statement: Scalar inequality divides into superiority, expressed with comparative -er or analytic more, and inferiority, expressed with less; scalar equality is typically expressed with as.
rules.condition: For a scalar degree comparison, classify an -er/more form as grammatical superiority and a less form as grammatical inferiority relative to the scale named by the compared predicate, rather than regarding less as another way to mark comparative inflection.

contrast.text: The steel beam is heavier than the timber beam. [-er superiority]
The method is more reliable than the older method. [analytic superiority]
The alternative is less reliable than the older method. [inferiority]
The steel beam is as heavy as the timber beam. [equality]

sources.section: §1.1 Two cross-cutting distinctions: scalar vs non-scalar, equality vs inequality

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: superiority versus inferiority in scalar inequality
burton_roberts_mapping.note: Burton-Roberts source material and concept index were not available for comparison; no Burton-Roberts position is inferred.

rules.review_notes: Human approval is explicitly given by the user's Chapter 13 request; no independent second-pass AI review was performed. This record must not be used as an automatic grammar-error prohibition.

rules.statement: The superiority/inferiority distinction is grammatical, while the direction of the measured scale is determined by the lexical meaning of the compared adjective; a comparative such as younger is still grammatically a superiority comparison.
rules.condition: When classifying a graded comparative, use the form -er/more versus less to identify grammatical superiority or inferiority, and separately interpret whether the lexical property orients the scale toward a larger or smaller physical value.

contrast.text: The younger cyclist was seventeen. [younger: grammatical superiority on the youth-oriented scale]
The older cyclist was nineteen. [older: grammatical superiority on the age-oriented scale]
The route is less narrow than the old one. [grammatical inferiority despite greater width]
The route is narrower than the old one. [grammatical superiority despite lesser width]

sources.section: §1.1 Two cross-cutting distinctions: scalar vs non-scalar, equality vs inequality

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Burton-Roberts source material and concept index were not available for comparison; no Burton-Roberts position is inferred.

rules.review_notes: The reference point is the lexical scale, not a universal physical-more-than ordering. In particular younger is still superiority although the age is lower; source p. 1100.

rules.statement: An unnegated scalar equality comparison normally sets a lower bound: the compared degree is at least that of the comparison standard and may exceed it, rather than necessarily being exactly equal.
rules.condition: When interpreting an affirmative scalar as ... as comparison without a contextual requirement for exact identity of measurement, treat it as excluding inferiority but allowing equality or superiority; allow context to strengthen the pragmatic suggestion of exact equality.

exceptions.description: Certain forms and discourse contexts strongly favour, or pragmatically suggest, an exact-equality interpretation even though the ordinary scalar equality comparison supplies a lower bound.

contrast.text: Nina is as quick as Paulo; she may be quicker. [equality comparison permits superiority]
The new engine is as efficient as the old one. [at least equal efficiency]
The student made as many as twenty corrections. [number expression may strongly suggest the stated exact count]
The new bridge is as wide as the old bridge, perhaps even wider. [lower-bound semantics]

sources.section: §1.1 Two cross-cutting distinctions: scalar vs non-scalar, equality vs inequality

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Burton-Roberts source material and concept index were not available for comparison; no Burton-Roberts position is inferred.

rules.review_notes: The source says normally and notes contextual variation; equative is the traditional term but Cambridge also treats the construction as comparative. Do not infer that as ... as always means exact equality.

rules.concept: ordinary negation of scalar equality yields inferiority
rules.statement: Under ordinary truth-functional negation, denying an as ... as scalar comparison entails that the compared degree is lower than the standard; metalinguistic negation may instead reject the wording as insufficiently strong while the degree is higher.
rules.condition: Where a scalar equality comparison is directly negated, distinguish ordinary negation of the lower-bound relation from metalinguistic correction of an overly weak assertion; only the ordinary-negation interpretation entails inferiority.

exceptions.description: Metalinguistic negation can reject as ... as as an insufficient description and follow it with an assertion of superiority, rather than entailing inferiority.

contrast.text: Lena isn't as patient as Omar. [ordinary negation: Lena is less patient]
The new model isn't as quiet as the prototype. [ordinary negation: less quiet]
The new model isn't as quiet as the prototype—it's much quieter! [metalinguistic correction, not ordinary denial]

rules.review_notes: Footnote 4 on p. 1101 explicitly points to Chapter 9 §1.2 for metalinguistic negation. The main-text entailment is explicitly restricted to ordinary negation.

rules.statement: Negatively oriented any/ever-type items are licensed by scalar inequality, scalar equality and non-scalar inequality comparatives, but non-scalar equality by itself does not provide the same licensing in the illustrated negative-polarity reading.
rules.condition: When interpreting a negative-polarity sense of any, anyone, anything or ever in a comparison, check the comparative subtype: scalar inequality, scalar equality or non-scalar inequality can supply a licensing environment even without overt clause negation, while a plain affirmative non-scalar same ... as comparison normally cannot without another licenser.

exceptions.description: Free-choice senses of any and independent negative-polarity licensers are distinct from the negative-polarity use in these plain affirmative comparison examples; absence of comparative licensing is not a ban on every surface sequence same ... as any.

contrast.text: The cyclist finished faster than anyone had predicted. [scalar inequality licenses anyone]
She climbed as high as she had ever climbed before. [scalar equality licenses ever]
The solution was different from anything we had previously tried. [non-scalar inequality licenses anything]
?The solution was the same as anything we had previously tried. [non-scalar equality does not itself license the intended negative-polarity reading]
